item.title: 增加隐私和安全相关声明和功能，方便企业用户使用
item.body:
在国外公司，正在尝试各种新的IDE并引入公司，请添加一个类似关于隐私和安全方面的声明或者类似于Cursor的Privacy mode功能，参考https://www.cursor.com/security 和 https://codeium.com/security ，让公司的信息安全，合规和Devops能够评估使用

请先添加声明方便开始评估，然后考虑增加类似功能

comments.body:
目前可以在官网中查阅隐私政策
感谢反馈，我们会尽快增加相关功能

好的，不过我尝试用AI对比了一下和其他几家的（如下），似乎还是不够强，建议你们可以考虑出一个针对企业用户的隐私说明页面或者FAQ，方便说服部门尝试使用

> Cursor: Cursor emphasizes robust privacy measures, detailed on its [Security page](https://www.cursor.com/security). It offers an optional Privacy Mode (enabled during onboarding or settings), ensuring no plaintext code is stored on servers or by subprocessors, with data only held in memory for request duration (minutes to hours for caching). About 50% of users enable this, and it’s mandatory for team members. Cursor is SOC 2 compliant, uses AWS hosting primarily in the US, and processes data with partners like OpenAI and Fireworks, but Privacy Mode prevents persistent storage. Non-privacy mode users’ data may be logged (e.g., via Datadog) or used for debugging, but sensitive data risks are minimized. User feedback praises its transparency, though some note complexity in extension security (e.g., unverified signatures).
Windsurf: Windsurf, from Codeium, prioritizes privacy with a privacy-first philosophy, as per [Codeium’s Windsurf page](https://codeium.com/windsurf). It offers SOC 2 Type II compliance and optional zero-day data retention for enterprise users, ensuring code isn’t stored long-term. Users can opt out of telemetry via settings, and no non-permissive data trains its models. Encryption secures data in transit, and self-hosted AI options exist for enterprises, appealing to privacy-conscious teams. Posts on X and blogs (e.g., DEV Community) highlight Windsurf’s edge over Cursor for free-tier privacy, though some users demand explicit opt-out for AI training, suggesting room for improvement compared to Cursor’s Privacy Mode clarity.
Trae: Developed by ByteDance, Trae’s privacy policy, available at [Trae IDE](https://traeide.com/), raises significant concerns, especially given its Chinese origins and TikTok-related scrutiny. It grants ByteDance broad, perpetual rights to use, modify, and distribute user code for “product improvement” and “business operations,” including AI training, with limited opt-out options. Data falls under Chinese regulations, potentially allowing government access, as noted in reviews like [Trae Review by Balazs Barta](https://www.hellobala.co/). Posts on X (e.g., @casparfrey) and Reddit threads express alarm over code security, with sentiments like “I don’t want my code stolen by China.” While Trae advises against sharing sensitive data, its policy lacks Cursor’s or Windsurf’s robust safeguards, making it riskier for proprietary work despite being free.
JetBrains IDEA: IDEA’s privacy policy, outlined at [JetBrains Privacy](https://www.jetbrains.com/legal/docs/privacy/privacy/), focuses on traditional IDE data handling, not AI-specific risks. It collects usage data for improvement (opt-out available) and complies with GDPR and CCPA, storing data in the EU or US based on user location. AI Assistant data may be processed by third-party providers (e.g., OpenAI), but JetBrains ensures contractual protections. No broad code usage rights are claimed, and its non-agentic AI reduces data-sharing needs compared to the others. It’s less AI-invasive but lacks the explicit privacy modes of Cursor or Windsurf, relying on established trust as a legacy tool.
Key Privacy Insights: Trae’s policy is indeed “different” and riskier, granting ByteDance extensive rights over code with weaker user control, aligning with ByteDance’s data-driven model (e.g., TikTok concerns). Cursor and Windsurf offer stronger privacy assurances—Cursor with its Privacy Mode and Windsurf with zero-day retention—while IDEA takes a conservative, non-AI-centric approach.

好的，非常感谢您的建议～
